# Ambient Dimension

## One-sentence definition

The **ambient dimension** is the dimension of the surrounding coordinate or vector space in which states, observations, or a candidate structure are represented.

## Why this concept matters

Ambient dimension records how many coordinates the chosen representation provides, not how many degrees of freedom the represented system actually uses. Keeping those questions separate prevents high-dimensional recordings from being equated with high intrinsic complexity.

## Intuition

A curve drawn in three-dimensional space has ambient dimension three even though motion along the curve may require only one local coordinate.

## Formal definition

If an object is represented as a subset $S\subseteq\mathbb R^D$, then $D$ is the ambient dimension of that representation. Changing the representation can change $D$ without changing the underlying object.

For a data matrix with $D$ measured features, $D$ is often the observation-space ambient dimension. This does not make the observations a complete state.

## Core notation

- $\mathbb R^D$: ambient coordinate space.
- $D$: ambient dimension.
- $S\subseteq\mathbb R^D$: represented set.

## Prerequisites

[State Space](state-space.qmd) establishes that a space and its coordinates depend on a declared system description.

## Relationship to adjacent concepts

| Concept | Distinction |
|---|---|
| **Intrinsic dimension** | Degrees of freedom assigned to the object under a model or criterion, not the surrounding coordinate count. |
| **Number of observations** | Sample count is not coordinate dimension. |
| **Rank** | A linear-algebraic property of a matrix or map that may be below ambient dimension. |
| **State dimension** | Dimension of a specified state representation; an observation space can have a different ambient dimension. |

## What this does NOT imply

Ambient dimension does not imply intrinsic dimension, manifold structure, effective rank, independent coordinates, mechanistic variables, or adequate sampling of the space.

## Minimal example

The unit circle represented in $\mathbb R^2$ has ambient dimension two. The same circle embedded in $\mathbb R^3$ has ambient dimension three although its local degree of freedom remains one.

## Neuroscience / behavioral relevance

The number of recorded neurons, sensors, time bins, or engineered features can define an ambient data dimension. It does not determine latent dimensionality.

## Relevance to LDG

Ambient Dimension supplies the reference quantity needed for careful claims about dimension reduction, subspaces, embeddings, and manifolds.

## Open questions

- Which preprocessing steps change the declared ambient space?
- Should missing or constrained coordinates count toward $D$?
- Which representation is appropriate for cross-modal comparisons?

## References

- Levina and Bickel explicitly distinguish high-dimensional embedding from lower intrinsic dimension in their inspected estimator study [@LevinaBickel2004].

- [x] Separates ambient dimension from samples, rank, and intrinsic dimension.
